title: Counting work and Big O
summary: Count how many items an algorithm checks. Meet Big O with a tiny search and learn why input size matters more than a stopwatch reading.
introduction: Looking for a pencil in three boxes is quick. Looking in three thousand boxes may take much longer. We can compare plans by counting how the work grows as we add more boxes.
learningObjectives: Count checks in a simple search
Separate an exact count from a Big O label

blocks.text: The **input size**, often called n, is how many items we give an algorithm. Here n is the number of scores in an array.
**Big O** is a label for an upper bound on how work grows. We usually ask about the worst case: the input that makes the plan do the most work for that size. It is not an exact number of seconds.
**O(1)** means the work stays bounded as n grows. Reading one known array position is an example. **O(n)** means a bound grows in line with n. Checking every item once is an example.
The program counts equality checks, not every tiny computer instruction. That gives us a simple measure we can follow. Real running time also depends on the language, device, and input.

items: Look for 9 in the scores 3, 6, and 9. Start checks at 0.
Check 3: it is not 9. The count becomes 1.
Check 6: it is not 9. The count becomes 2.
Check 9: it matches. The count becomes 3, so stop and print 3.

blocks.text: Choose one tab. All six programs do the same task and print the same result. JavaScript can run here. The other languages need the separate local tools in [Language setup](/tutorials/data-structures-algorithms/language-setup).

blocks.title: Counting work and Big O example

variants.caption: Run this JavaScript in the browser playground, or save main.js and use Node.js.
Use a separate local C11 compiler. Save this complete program as main.c; see Language setup.
Use a separate local C++17 compiler. Save this complete program as main.cpp; see Language setup.

variants.code:
scores = [3, 6, 9]
target = 9
checks = 0
for score in scores:
    checks += 1
    if score == target:
        break
print(checks)

Use a separate local .NET 8 or newer console project. Replace Program.cs with this complete program.
Use a separate local JDK 17 or newer. Save this complete program as Main.java; see Language setup.

blocks.text: There are exactly 3 checks for this input. With n scores, an absent target or a target at the end needs n checks. This search has O(n) worst-case work. Finding the first item takes only one check.
Check the small and tricky cases
If there are no items, there are no checks. If the target appears twice, this program stops at the first match. The count alone does not tell us whether a match was found.

**O(n²)**, read O of n squared, often appears when we check every pair. With 3 items there are 3 × 3 ordered pairs if self-pairs are included. Do not label every two-loop program O(n²): two separate scans still have O(n) growth.
An algorithm also uses space, which means extra storage. This search uses a counter and a target: O(1) extra space, apart from the input array.

items: Change target from 9 to 3. Predict how many checks happen.
The output becomes 1. This faster input does not change the O(n) worst-case label for the search.

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.text: Do not read O(n) as exactly n seconds. Big O describes growth. A tiny example can be fast even when its plan grows poorly.
